body.text: On November 2-3, the Kazakhstan government hosted the Second Tianshan Forum for Central Asian Economic Cooperation in Almaty. The forum, whose theme was “Strengthening Resilient Connectivity and Quality Investment in Central Asia,” brought together regional officials, business representatives, think tanks and development organizations from more than ten countries, including those in Central Asia, as well as Georgia, China and Pakistan.

Participants at the Tianshan Forum discussed how to enhance regional economic cooperation, investment and digital connectivity. Pakistan presented its seaports as potential gateways for landlocked Central Asian economies. Addressing the opening session of the forum, Pakistan’s Minister for the Board of Investment, Qaisar Ahmed Sheikh, drew attention to Pakistani ports at Karachi, Gwadar and Qasim as strategic gateways to facilitate maritime trade and provide landlocked Kazakhstan with alternative routes for the movement of goods.

This is not the first time that Pakistan and Kazakhstan have shown interest in trade cooperation. In February 2026, during Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s state visit to Islamabad, a joint business forum brought together government representatives, business organizations and private sector actors. The forum resulted in 37 commercial agreements between the two countries and a joint declaration establishing a strategic partnership.

At the February 2026 meeting, Kazakhstan and Pakistan discussed the need to develop regional connectivity and establish alternate routes linking Central Asia with the Indian Ocean. One of the proposals envisaged connecting Turgundi and Herat in Afghanistan to Spin Boldak near the Pakistan border. This could potentially provide Kazakhstan with access to the Indian Ocean via Pakistan. The three possible routes being considered include a route through China, the Trans-Afghan corridor via Uzbekistan and Afghanistan, and a potential route through Iran via Bandar Abbas. Given their proximity to Balochistan, the routes through Afghanistan and Iran could connect to Gwadar.

For Pakistan, the proposed connectivity is an economic opportunity. The ports at Karachi and Qasim are already established and busy commercial and industrial gateways. Gwadar Port, on the other hand, has been underutilized since its launch in 2007. The plan was to develop it as a regional transshipment and logistics hub. But the port’s commercial performance is yet to match ambitions. In terms of business, Gwadar has yet to reach even a fraction of the scale at which ports in Dubai, Salalah, or even Karachi are operating.

While Gwadar’s proximity to the Strait of Hormuz brought a temporary surge in business amid the U.S.-Iran war, relying on exceptional periods of regional disruptions is not sustainable for consistent cargo flows. Regardless, given Gwadar’s potential, Pakistan has been persistent in promoting Gwadar to many countries in the past. Pakistan’s fragile economic situation underlies this persistence. It is with this in mind that Pakistan is eyeing Kazakhstan as a partner.
As for Kazakhstan, it is keen to improve connectivity and access to the Indian Ocean. This interest has gained momentum in recent years.

In April 2025, Kazakhstan signed a protocol of intent with Afghanistan to construct the Turgundi-Herat-Kandahar-Spin Boldak railway line. However, this proposed corridor is not operational yet. Since Turgundi is at the Afghan-Turkmen border, and there is an established railway line between Kazakhstan and Turkmenistan, Kazakhstan would not have to build an entirely new railway line. It would only need to extend the railway line toward Afghanistan and then eventually toward Pakistan.

For more than three decades, Kazakhstan has followed a multivector foreign policy. The Central Asian nation is keen to build relations with global and regional powers even as it preserves its strategic autonomy.

A landlocked country that shares a 7,800-km border with Russia (the world’s second-longest border) and a 1,700-km border with China, and situated at the crossroads of Eurasia, Kazakhstan is keen not only to diversify its economic and diplomatic relations but also to reduce its dependence on a single route for trade, as relying on a single route could expose its economy to geopolitical and logistical vulnerabilities.

Currently, around 80 percent of Kazakhstan’s oil exports rely on the Caspian Pipeline Consortium (CPC), which passes westward through Russia all the way to Black Sea via Novorossiysk port. From there, the oil is shipped by tankers through the Turkish Straits to the international market. Other important routes for Kazakh oil exports are the Atyrau-Samara pipeline that goes northward to Russia, the Atasu-Alashankou pipeline passing through China, and the Caspian Sea route through the Kazakh port of Aktau.

However, reliance on these routes has been both a blessing for Kazakhstan and a curse. Although these routes have, without doubt, provided it with access to international markets, Kazakhstan’s trade has been disrupted multiple times in recent years. Its dependence on Russian routes has brought repeated disruptions since the start of the Ukraine-Russia war in 2022.

For example, in February 2025, Ukrainian drones hit the Kropotkinskaya oil pumping station, which is on the Russian section of the CPC pipeline. Similarly, in November that year, a Ukrainian sea-drone attack on Russia’s Novorossiysk port suspended oil loadings. Such attacks have continued since.

Kazakhstan is the world’s 12th largest crude oil producer, and oil accounts for around 51 percent of its total earnings from exports. Hence, more than any other commodity, it is oil that Kazakhstan is interested in exporting. Since the U.S.-Iran war, the demand for non-Gulf oil supplies has also increased. This has increased pressure as well as created an opportunity for Kazakhstan to export its oil and emerge as a beneficiary of the situation. However, increasing production alone does not help if its oil cannot be transported to international markets.

Apart from crude oil, Astana also exports automobiles, and other machinery, copper, uranium, aluminum and other precious metals and pharmaceuticals. Kazakhstan recently announced plans to increase pharmaceutical exports.

Kazakhstan is therefore looking for alternative export routes and is increasing its cooperation with neighboring and regional countries. As the world’s largest crude oil importer, China relies heavily on Kazakhstan, and the two countries are looking to expand existing cross-border pipeline infrastructure.

Therefore, China was an important guest at the recent Tianshan Forum. But, following the multivector foreign policy, Kazakhstan is looking to expand its connections across multiple transport networks, and not necessarily relying on a single trade partner or transit corridor, especially in a world that is exposed to disruptions more often than ever.

From a political economy perspective, the impact of such disruptions is different for exporters and importers. If an importer cannot get a product from one country, it may be able to buy it from another supplier. But for an exporter, having a product is not enough; it needs reliable routes to reach international markets as well as dependable partners for cooperation.

In this context, Kazakhstan’s interest in Pakistan is about not only expanding its trade routes but also diversifying its transit corridors, so it has more options to access its existing and new markets. Pakistan, thus, potentially provides an important connection to the Arabian Sea through its three sea ports.

Kazakhstan’s increased interest in Pakistan is evident from the growing number of Kazakh officials visiting the country and the increasing frequency of diplomatic meetings focusing on trade and investment.

At a meeting on November 18, Kazakh and Pakistani officials pledged to increase trade to $1 billion in the next five years. However, trade and investment plans seem rather ambitious, as translating pledges into reality can be complicated given Pakistan’s internal security challenges. Pakistan’s ongoing military conflict with Afghanistan adds to the complexities, and the other route via Iran is also currently not feasible given the ongoing U.S-Iran war.

Thus, the prospects of connecting Iran or Afghanistan and Pakistan via Kazakhstan’s proposed railway project and Kazakhstan’s ambition to access the Indian Ocean via Pakistani ports seem constrained by ongoing political and security situations.
For Pakistan, a partnership with Kazakhstan is an opportunity to develop a new regional transit corridor and perhaps make use of Gwadar Port, which has so far been underutilized.

However, without political stability and security, the proposed Pakistan-Kazakhstan trade corridor will remain just a dream. It will be another addition to the long list of unrealized connectivity projects.
